Before she begins, she casts Protection from Evil and Good on Corm, since his hand is the one on the stone, and says softly, "Steady, old friend. I'm here."

Then she begins the Naming in a low, clear voice, saying the Morninglord's invocation first, and then each of the sixty names slowly, one at a time, with Brenn Ironvein's last.

input.add_to_description: Dawn Day 4: the Naming spoken (Religion 17). The sixty named, Brenn last; Protection from Evil and Good on Corm. The door opened and the sleeper was released with mercy. Brun's duty now: the bound dead, burial, and the hold's memory; hooks: Dorrin's hidden letters to the Deepwatch, Sigrun's iron ring.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

You lay your palm on Corm's shoulder and speak the Protection over him. A faint, silvery warmth settles on his skin like a second cloak. He breathes out and nods once.

Then you read. The Morninglord's invocation first, low and even, and the iron under your holy symbol grows warm. You give the names one at a time, in the captain's order, each set down like a stone in a cairn. The tunnel seems to lean in and listen. Somewhere around the thirtieth, the hum in your teeth changes: not louder, but deeper, almost a voice, almost a sigh. Hild's lips move silently with every name. Garrick, at the bend, has taken off his hood.

You come to the last. "Brenn Ironvein." Hild makes a small, broken sound, and you say it again, gently. "Brenn Ironvein, who stayed to hold its hand."

The heartstone flares, a soft gold the color of morning through shutters, and the lines on the door burn bright and then slowly go out one by one, like lamps at the end of a long vigil. The iron groans, and the door swings inward on its own.

There is no rush of horror. Warm air moves past you, smelling of rain on stone and old wood-smoke, and a vast, slow presence passes through the gallery and out, like a held breath finally let go. Dust lifts in the lamplight and settles. Down the stair beyond, faint and many, you hear something like footsteps, unhurried, going up and away: the sixty, walking home.

Corm sinks to his knees with his hand still on the stone, weeping openly. Hild kneels beside him and puts her arm around his shoulders. The stone in the door goes dark and quiet, only a stone.

The hold is open and still. The Morninglord's light is coming faint and gold down the tunnel mouth, and beyond the door the lower galleries wait, to be walked and the dead honored. Your protection will fade in minutes. What does Brun do?

sheet.opening: Brunhilde "Brun" Stonehearth, a stocky Hill Dwarf cleric of the Morninglord (Life domain), auburn braid threaded with brass beads, dented but polished chain mail, warhammer worn smooth at the grip, carries the prayer book of her late foster-father figure, Father Dorrin Ashbeard, the old priest who found her as a half-starved orphan in a collapsed mine shaft outside a hill-hold and raised her in his small shrine. input.add_to_description: Dawn Day 4: Brun cast Protection from Evil and Good on Corm and began the Naming (Religion 7 vs DC 12, failed). Around the fortieth name her voice caught and she lost the thread; the sleeper stirred and the door shuddered, the heartstone flared. The rite is unfinished but not broken: Corm holds. She can resume from the name she lost.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

A pale shimmer settles over Corm like frost on a window, and he draws a long breath. "Aye," he whispers. "Go on."

You begin. The invocation of the Morninglord comes out clear and warm, and the first names follow, one by one, each dropped into the cold gallery like a stone into a deep well. With each, the heartstone beside Corm's hand glows a little brighter, and the door's iron bands answer with a low, trembling note. Hild's lips move silently with you. Garrick stands at the bend, very still.

Somewhere past the fortieth name, the thread slips. You see a name in Father Dorrin's book that the captain's order has put twice, or perhaps you only think you do, and your tongue trips on a syllable. The note in the door goes sour.

The heartstone flares white. The iron shudders from top to bottom and a deep groan rises through the floor, not anger so much as a great startled breath, and grit rains from the ceiling timbers. Beyond the door something vast turns over in the dark. Corm's whole arm shakes to the shoulder, but his hand does not leave the stone and Protection from Evil and Good holds around him, for ten minutes at most.

The rite is not broken, only stumbling, and the names you have spoken still hang in the air. You are at the forty-first name. Nineteen remain, and Brenn's is last. Three slots became two, and the shimmer on Corm needs your concentration to hold.

What does Brun do?

input.add_to_description: Dawn Day 4 ~6:20 AM: Brun spoke the Naming with Protection from Evil and Good on Corm (Insight 22). The sleeper answered gently: the door's hum rose into a long exhale and the seal began to release; the door stands closed but unbarred. Names answered by faint knocks from beyond; Brenn's name answered by a hand pressed to the iron.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

Your hand finds Corm's shoulder, the ward settles over him like a held breath, and you begin.

The Morninglord's invocation comes first, and the old words are plain and warm in your mouth. Then the names, one at a time, slowly, as if each were someone you had known. You do not hurry. Between names you listen, and the door listens back.

Somewhere around the twentieth, the hum in your teeth changes. It is no longer a drone but something with a shape, rising and falling like a long, tired breath. By the fortieth you can feel it through the iron under your palm, not a threat but a weight, as if something vast were leaning close to hear. You understand then what the captain wrote. It is not angry. It is afraid, and it has been for forty winters, and nobody has said the names of those who stayed with it.

At each name there is a soft knock from the far side of the door, a single one, patient, like a knuckle on wood. Sixty names, sixty knocks. Hild's lips move with every one, and Corm's eyes are shut, and the tears run into his beard without a sound.

Last, you say it: "Brenn Ironvein."

For a moment, nothing. Then a hand presses flat against the iron from the other side. You see it more than hear it, a faint warm shape in the cold metal, wide-fingered and broad, exactly the size of a miner's. Hild makes a sound you will not forget and puts her own palm against the place.

The heartstone loosens in its socket with a sigh. The hum goes out of the air like a held note let go, and the cold, sweet smell does not return. The great door is still closed, but you can feel it is no longer barred. It stands against the dawn as a door should, and not as a wall.

Corm lifts his scarred hand from the stone. The old brand on his arm has faded to a pale line. "It's done," he whispers. "It let go."

The ward on him has ended, spent, and nobody is in danger. Your spell slots are at two of three. The way beyond the door is open if you choose to go, and Hild is waiting for you to say whether you will go together.

Brun steps up to the door beside Corm, opens Father Dorrin's prayer book to the captain's rite, and sets her holy symbol against the cold iron. Before she begins, she casts Protection from Evil and Good on Corm, since his hand is the one on the stone, and says softly, "Steady, old friend. I'm here."

input.add_to_description: Dawn Day 4: the Naming was spoken (Religion 16). All sixty names said, Brenn last, Corm's hand on the heartstone under Protection from Evil and Good. The sleeper did not wake in anger: the door's seams glowed and the stone-spirit was released with mercy. The door stands unbarred. The way below is open; Corm and Hild mean to go down and bring up the sixty to be buried. Quest essentially complete.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

You lay your holy symbol against the cold iron and touch Corm's shoulder. The warding settles over him like a held breath, and you speak the Morninglord's invocation. Your voice does not shake.

Then the names. Brun, you say them one at a time, slowly, as if each were a family member walking through a door. At the twentieth the iron under your hand warms. At the fortieth the heartstone's dull glow begins to brighten, gold and soft, like sunrise through a shutter. Corm stands with his scarred arm braced and his eyes shut, and his lips move with every name. Hild's tears run unchecked into her beard, and she does not wipe them.

At the fifty-ninth, the whole door sighs. A long, low note rises through the stone, neither anger nor hunger but something closer to a child's breath after a long night of weeping. You finish the list. Last, you say: "Brenn Ironvein. Who stayed. Who held its hand."

The gold floods up through the door's seams, the iron bands loosen with a sound like old ice breaking, and the door swings an inch inward on its own. A wind comes out of the dark, cool and clean and smelling of wet stone and rain. It goes past you up the tunnel and out toward the dawn, and the hum in your teeth is gone for good.

Do you want to level up now, or first see what Corm and Hild decide to do next?

line:
Brun falls into step beside Maren and shortens her stride to match. "Aunt Maren, while we walk, would you tell me about the Deepwatch itself, and about my mother as a girl? I'd like to hear the small things, like what she liked to eat and what songs she sang."

She glances ahead at Garrick and adds, "Garrick, thank you for the ford and the sheep trail. At the waymark-hut tonight I'll cook, since you've done the hard work all day."

input.add_to_description: Told by Maren on the road (Day 5): as a girl Sigrun hummed the mine-counting song while she worked, ate honey-oat cakes with too much salt, climbed every cairn on the Deepwatch's long wall, and drew maps on her own bedroom wall with charcoal until she was given a proper slate. She sang 'The Lamp Below' (a warden's lullaby) and made up a second verse of her own for her daughter.

Maren's account (Day 5): a fortress-hall cut into the north face of a mountain called the Anvil, a long wall of cairns before it, a great lamp lit at every dusk for the wardens still below. A hall of names, with a book for every hold. Fewer than forty wardens remain.

entries.text: time: 4 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 6:59 PM

Maren is quiet for a dozen paces, and you begin to think she will not answer. Then the words come, a little at a time, in step with her staff.

"The Deepwatch is cut into the north face of a mountain we call the Anvil," she says. "A long wall of cairns runs before it, one for each warden who went below and did not come home. At every dusk a great lamp is lit in the high window for them, so they may find the way. We are fewer than forty now. But the hall of names is full."

Then she tells you the small things you asked for. Sigrun hummed the mine-counting song under her breath whenever she worked, so that you could always find her in a crowd by the sound. She ate honey-oat cakes with far too much salt in them and would hear no argument. She climbed every cairn on the long wall before she was ten, and drew maps on her bedroom wall in charcoal until the cooks, in despair, gave her a proper slate. She sang a lullaby called *The Lamp Below*, and when you were born she made up a second verse for it, which she never wrote down.

"I have never heard it," Maren says. "But I think you might."

You walk on a while without speaking, the hum of the wind in the grass, and then Maren begins to sing the first verse, low and cracked, and you find that you know the tune. Not the words, only the shape of it, somewhere under your ribs.

The waymark-hut comes into view at dusk: a squat round tower of fitted stone on the saddle, roofed in turf, with a warden's hammer carved over a low door. Inside it is dry and has a hearth, a stack of split wood left by whoever passed before, a bench, and three narrow cots. You cook, as you promised: oatmeal with dried apple, and a rasher of Garrick's smoked ham fried in its own fat, and a little salt, which Maren eats with great approval.

You are at 21 of 21, with three slots, and nothing has troubled you on the road. Outside, the stars are coming out over the high hills, and the Deepwatch is a day and a half off.

What does Brun do?

Per Maren (Day 5): built into a cliff-face above a glacial lake; a long stair of nine hundred steps, a great ledger-hall called the Hall of Names, and a gate that is only opened to a warden's kin-sign. entries.text:
Maren is quiet for a few dozen paces, then begins, her voice finding the rhythm of her staff on the stones.

The Deepwatch, she says, is built into a cliff-face above a lake that is ice-green all year, with a stair of nine hundred steps cut up to its gate and a gate that opens only to the wardens' kin-sign. Inside is the Hall of Names, where every hold's dead are written on slate. Fewer than forty wardens keep it now, and they keep it badly, she admits, being old and stubborn.

Then she talks about your mother, and it is the small things you asked for. Sigrun chalked maps on every flat stone she could find, and was scolded for it, and did it anyway. She hated turnips and would trade a whole week's pudding to avoid them. She loved honey-oat cakes, and baked them badly. She sang the miners' round, "Down the Long Stair," off-key on purpose, because it made the old cooks throw spoons. "You have her mouth when you frown," Maren says. "I saw it at the shrine last night, when you thought no one was looking."

You walk a long while with that, and Garrick, ahead, does not turn around.

When you stop to check your pack for the waterskin, you find something you had not seen tucked inside the back cover of Father Dorrin's book: two folded letters, sealed in grey wax with the old priest's thumb-ring, and addressed in his cramped hand to the Hall of Names at the Deepwatch. Maren looks at them and says only, "Then he did write more than once. Keep them. They are for the hall, and perhaps for you."

The waymark-hut comes into view at half past five, a squat round stone shelter at the saddle with a turf roof, a hearth, and a cairn of three stones at its door. Garrick checks it for tracks and finds none but a goat's. The wind has turned cold. You have the oatcakes, the dried apple, and Garrick's rations, and you said you would cook.

What does Brun do?

entries.text:
Maren is quiet for a few paces, and then she begins, and does not stop for hours.

She tells you of the Deepwatch first, because it is easier. It is a hall cut into the face of a cliff above a gorge so deep the river at the bottom is only a sound. One stair and one rope bridge reach it. Inside is the Hall of Names, where every ledger of every hold is kept, and where the lost are written down so the stone will remember them. There are fewer than forty wardens left, most of them old. Their captain is a stubborn, grey-bearded dwarf named Brokk Hallowforge, who she says "will growl at you, and you must not mind it."

Then she tells you of your mother, in small things, the way you asked. Sigrun loved honeyed barley cakes and hated mutton so much she would trade a week of her wages to be spared it. She sang the warden's shaft-song, "Down by the line, up by the light," and sang it off-key on purpose to annoy her elders. As a girl she kept a jackdaw named Pebble that stole spoons. Once, when her lamp failed in a deep gallery, she mapped the whole of it by touch and dead reckoning in the dark, and came out and told no one she had been afraid. Maren only knew because she found the map, with the corners smudged where a hand had gripped too hard.

You laugh at the jackdaw, and then you do not, and Maren puts her dry hand over yours for a few steps and says nothing.

By the time the light turns gold and long you have come to the saddle, a bare notch between two hills where a low stone hut crouches with a turf roof and a hearth. It is a warden's waymark-hut, the hammer brand burned into its lintel, a woodpile stacked inside and a clean floor. Garrick checks the corners, the roof, the hearth flue, and nods.

You cook, as you promised: oatcakes, a stew of dried apple and salt pork, and the last of the cheese. Garrick eats without speaking and then, unexpectedly, says it is the best thing he has had on a road. Maren says the stew needs honey. You tell her it does.

It is half past six, with night coming on, and the wind rising a little off the saddle. The Deepwatch is a day and a half further. What does Brun do?

Your words ring off the cliff-face in the wind, and for a moment the sentry says nothing. Then the lantern swings. "Sigrun's girl," he says, as if testing the shape of it. "Hold there." He vanishes from the parapet.

Brun squares her shoulders, wipes the rain from her face, and calls up to the sentry in clear Dwarvish, "I'm Brunhilde Stonehearth, Sigrun's daughter, raised by Father Dorrin Ashbeard. I carry a copy of the Hearthdeep warden-captain's ledger, and I've come home."

entries.text:
The bronze doors have opened and Captain Torvald Greycairn has welcomed you and Garrick into the Deepwatch as guests. The notebook is now up to date, and the clock reads 5:39 PM.

What does Brun do?

The sentry lifts the lantern higher, and for a long breath there is only the wind. Then the bronze doors begin to open, inward, slowly, on a hall full of gold light.

Your pack holds the ledger in its dry cloth, Father Dorrin's book, and two sealed letters in his cramped hand that you had not noticed tucked behind the prayer book's binding. The wax bears the wardens' hammer, and both are addressed to the Deepwatch. You haven't read them, and they weren't yours to read before now.

A tall, stooped dwarf strides out under the arch, grey-bearded, in a captain's heavy cloak and a plain iron circlet. Torvald Greycairn, you guess, and his face is carved from the same stone as the doors. Behind him a few wardens gather with lanterns, and a small child peers round a leg.

He looks at Maren first, and something tightens in his jaw, a scolding he doesn't give. Then he looks at you for a very long time, at the braid, the chin, the ring on your smallest finger.

"Three days late," he says to Maren, rough. "And you bring the storm with you."

Then he turns to you and bows, very slightly, the bow one dwarf gives a kinswoman.

"Sigrun's daughter," he says. "The hall has kept a lamp lit for you for twenty years. Come in out of the rain, child, and bring the hunter. You are both guests of the Deepwatch."

Warmth rolls out of the gate: peat smoke, hot bread, lamp oil. Garrick glances at you, uncertain, and you can see he has never been welcomed anywhere so wholly.

It is a little past half past five. You are at 21 of 21 with three spell slots and Channel Divinity. What does Brun do?

sheet.opening: Brunhilde "Brun" Stonehearth, a stocky Hill Dwarf cleric of the Morninglord (Life domain), auburn braid threaded with brass beads, dented but polished chain mail, warhammer worn smooth at the grip, carries the prayer book of her late foster-father figure, Father Dorrin Ashbeard, the old priest who found her as a half-starved orphan in a collapsed mine shaft outside a hill-hold and raised her in his small shrine. She is optimistic, tries to find common ground even between fierce enemies, is suspicious of strangers, and wants to repay the mercy she was shown by walking into danger to keep others alive (ideal: Charity). Opening: it is late afternoon and Brun has just arrived at a rain-soaked crossroads waystation on a mountain road, a squat stone inn and shrine-lean-to shared by travelers, having come down from the hills to carry Father Dorrin's blessing to those in need. A fresh rockslide has just buried part of the road beyond the station, and muffled tapping and a faint cry for help are coming from beneath the stones: a wagon of travelers (a wounded merchant, a child, and a mule-driver) is trapped, and a group of wary, mismatched strangers (a nervous caravan guard, a sullen hunter, and the innkeeper) is arguing over whether it is safe to dig or whether the whole slope will come down. The hurt need a healer now, and the strangers need someone to pull them together before the mountain moves again. Brun, who knows exactly what it is to be trapped under stone and found, is the one they turn to. Her Stonecunning and Smith's Tools may help read the unstable rock and shore it up; her spells (Healing Word, Cure Wounds, Bless, Sanctuary) may keep people alive. Keep the backstory true: Father Dorrin raised her long ago and she carries his book; nothing about it is recent or lost.
